tweets: One rock. One sculptor's chisel. A 57-foot man standing silently on a hilltop in Karnataka for over a thousand years — and every 12 years, thousands climb up just to pour milk over his head.

This is Gomateshwara — known in Jain tradition as Bahubali — carved from a single outcrop of granite atop Vindhyagiri hill in Shravanabelagola, Karnataka. Commissioned around 981 CE by Chavundaraya, a minister and general under the Western Ganga dynasty.

Sculptors shaped the entire 17-metre figure from that one mass of stone — including the vines curling up his legs and arms, and the anthill at his feet, symbols of a meditation so long and so still that nature grew over him undisturbed.

Once every 12 years, the Mahamastakabhisheka unfolds: the statue's head is anointed with milk, turmeric, sandalwood, saffron paste and gold coins poured from towers built specially for the ceremony — still one of India's great living pilgrimages.

A thousand years after the first chisel strike, one block of stone still draws millions uphill just to look up at it. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
